title: The Bennington Women
text:
In the 1930s, Bennington College in Vermont was a new, small college for women. Most students came from wealthy, politically conservative families, but many of the faculty and older students were liberal, and the campus was alive with discussion of the New Deal, the Spanish Civil War and other public issues.

Theodore Newcomb, a social psychologist on the faculty, surveyed nearly all the students repeatedly from 1935 to 1939 to track their political and social attitudes. He found a steady shift. Freshmen tended to share their parents' conservative views, but with each year at Bennington, students became more liberal. In the 1936 presidential election, most first-year students favored the Republican candidate, Alf Landon, while most juniors and seniors favored Franklin Roosevelt or candidates further to the left.

The shift was strongest among students who were most involved in campus life and who looked to the college community as their reference group. Students who stayed closely tied to their families, or who were isolated on campus, changed less.

Newcomb and his colleagues later followed up with the same women in the 1960s and again decades after that. Many had kept their liberal views, often supported by husbands and friends who shared them.
lesson: People take on the views of the group they most want to belong to, and those views can last a lifetime. Choose your communities with care.
source: Newcomb, T. M. (1943). Personality and Social Change: Attitude Formation in a Student Community. Dryden Press.
